concepts.name: Balance of Payments (BoP): Overall Architecture and Current Account's Position
key_dimensions: Distinction between Current Account, Capital Account, and Financial Account within BoP
Why BoP always 'balances' technically vs. deficit/surplus in sub-accounts
Role of 'Errors and Omissions' and 'Reserve Account' as residual items
UPSC trap: Capital Account Convertibility vs. Current Account Convertibility — India's status on each

concepts.name: Trade in Goods (Merchandise Trade): Composition and Measurement
key_dimensions: Difference between Balance of Trade (BoT) and Current Account Balance — why BoT ≠ CAD
FOB (Free on Board) vs. CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) valuation and their asymmetric impact on trade statistics
India's chronic merchandise trade deficit: structural reasons (oil, gold, electronics)
UPSC trap: Visible vs. Invisible trade — goods are 'visible'; services are 'invisible' but both are in Current Account

concepts.name: Trade in Services: Composition and India's Comparative Advantage
key_dimensions: Four modes of services supply under GATS (Mode 1: Cross-border, Mode 2: Consumption abroad, Mode 3: Commercial presence, Mode 4: Movement of persons)
India's services surplus consistently offsetting merchandise deficit — software, IT-ITeS, business services
Travel, transportation, financial, and insurance services as sub-components
UPSC trap: Services trade is recorded in Current Account, NOT Capital Account — common confusion with FDI in services sector

concepts.name: Primary Income Account (formerly 'Income Account'): Factor Payments
key_dimensions: Components: compensation of employees (remittances by workers abroad ≠ primary income), investment income (dividends, interest, profits), and reserve asset income
UPSC trap: Worker remittances are in 'Secondary Income' (transfers), NOT Primary Income — a classic trap
India typically runs a deficit on Primary Income due to profit repatriation by MNCs exceeding returns on Indian assets abroad
Distinction between GNP and GDP linked to Primary Income flows (net factor income from abroad)

concepts.name: Secondary Income Account (Transfers): Remittances and Official Aid
key_dimensions: Components: personal transfers (remittances), government transfers (foreign aid grants), and pension transfers
India as world's largest recipient of remittances — role in financing CAD
Unilateral transfers: no quid pro quo — distinguishes them from loans (Capital Account) and investments
UPSC trap: Foreign aid as GRANT goes to Secondary Income (Current Account); foreign aid as LOAN goes to Capital/Financial Account

concepts.name: Current Account Deficit (CAD): Meaning, Financing, and Sustainability
key_dimensions: CAD = (Imports of goods + services + primary income payments + secondary income payments) minus corresponding credits
Financing mechanisms: FDI, FPI, ECBs, NRI deposits, forex reserve drawdown — sustainability depends on financing quality
Threshold debate: CAD above 3% of GDP considered unsustainable for India — 2012-13 crisis context
UPSC trap: A CAD is not inherently bad if financed by productive FDI; a surplus is not inherently good (e.g., deflationary impact)

concepts.name: Twin Deficit Hypothesis: Fiscal Deficit and Current Account Deficit Linkage
key_dimensions: Theoretical link: Fiscal deficit → excess domestic demand → higher imports → CAD (Keynesian absorption approach)
National income identity: CAD = (I - S) + (G - T) — investment-savings gap plus fiscal deficit
Empirical validity contested for India — periods where twin deficits diverged
UPSC trap: Twin deficit is a hypothesis/tendency, not a universal law — exceptions matter for analytical questions

concepts.name: Invisibles in Current Account: Definition, Components, and India's Surplus
key_dimensions: Invisibles = Services + Primary Income + Secondary Income (everything except merchandise goods)
India's invisibles surplus has historically been large enough to partially offset merchandise deficit
Sub-components: software exports, tourism receipts, remittances, financial services
UPSC trap: 'Invisibles surplus' does NOT mean India has a Current Account surplus — net position depends on magnitude of merchandise deficit

concepts.name: Remittances: Recording in BoP, Determinants, and Macroeconomic Impact
key_dimensions: Recorded under Secondary Income (Current Account), NOT Capital Account — despite being a cross-border financial flow
India's top remittance-sending countries: USA, UAE, Saudi Arabia, UK — diaspora geography matters
Counter-cyclical nature: remittances often rise during domestic recessions as diaspora supports families
UPSC trap: NRI deposits (NRE, NRO, FCNR accounts) are in Capital/Financial Account; only personal transfers are in Current Account

concepts.name: Gold Imports and Their Impact on Current Account
key_dimensions: Gold is a merchandise import — directly worsens trade deficit and CAD
2013 measures: import duty hike to 10%, 80:20 scheme (80% domestic use, 20% re-export mandatory) — policy response context
Gold as 'non-productive' import vs. capital goods imports that enhance productive capacity
UPSC trap: Gold ETF purchases by residents are domestic financial transactions; physical gold imports affect Current Account

concepts.name: Oil Import Bill and Current Account Vulnerability
key_dimensions: India imports ~85% of crude oil needs — price and volume both affect CAD
Rule of thumb: Every $10/barrel rise in crude oil price widens CAD by ~$12-15 billion
Petrodollar recycling: oil-exporting nations' surpluses and their investment back into deficit nations
UPSC trap: Oil imports affect Current Account (merchandise), but hedging via derivatives affects Financial Account

concepts.name: Software and IT Services Exports: Mechanism of Recording in BoP
key_dimensions: Recorded under 'Services' within Current Account — specifically under 'Computer and Information Services'
India's IT exports primarily Mode 1 (cross-border supply) and Mode 4 (movement of persons) under GATS
Services exports do NOT involve physical movement of goods — no customs data; measured through banking channel/RBI surveys
UPSC trap: IT company setting up subsidiary abroad = FDI outflow (Financial Account); IT services revenue received = Current Account credit

concepts.name: Tourism and Travel Account: Receipts vs. Expenditure
key_dimensions: Foreign tourists spending in India = Credit (export of services); Indians spending abroad = Debit (import of services)
Part of 'Travel Services' under the Services component of Current Account
COVID-19 impact: collapse of travel account — illustrates volatility of this component
UPSC trap: Indian pilgrim spending at foreign religious sites = import of services (travel debit), not cultural exchange grant

concepts.name: Current Account Convertibility: Meaning, India's Status, and Exceptions
key_dimensions: IMF Article VIII: Current Account convertibility means no restrictions on payments for current international transactions
India accepted Article VIII obligations in 1994 — full current account convertibility achieved
Partial Capital Account convertibility: FDI is largely free, FPI has limits, full convertibility not yet achieved
UPSC trap: Current Account convertibility ≠ no import restrictions; tariffs are allowed; quantitative restrictions are what Article VIII restricts

concepts.name: Marshall-Lerner Condition and J-Curve Effect on Current Account
key_dimensions: Marshall-Lerner Condition: depreciation improves Current Account only if sum of price elasticities of exports and imports > 1
J-Curve: short-run worsening of CAD after depreciation (due to inelastic demand) before long-run improvement
India's context: high import inelasticity for oil and gold limits effectiveness of rupee depreciation on CAD
UPSC trap: Rupee depreciation always improves CAD — FALSE; depends on Marshall-Lerner condition being satisfied

concepts.name: Absorption Approach vs. Elasticity Approach to Current Account Adjustment
key_dimensions: Absorption Approach (Alexander): CAD = Domestic Expenditure (Absorption) − National Income; improvement requires cutting absorption or raising income
Elasticity Approach: focuses on relative prices and exchange rate effects on trade volumes
Policy implication: expenditure-switching (depreciation) vs. expenditure-reducing (fiscal contraction) policies
UPSC trap: IMF's structural adjustment programs use absorption approach — austerity rationale derives from this framework

concepts.name: Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) and Its Link to Primary Income Account
key_dimensions: NFIA = Factor income earned by residents abroad − Factor income paid to non-residents domestically
GNP = GDP + NFIA — this macroeconomic identity links National Accounts to BoP Current Account
For India, NFIA is typically negative (profit repatriation by MNCs > earnings on India's external assets)
UPSC trap: Remittances are NOT factor income and NOT part of NFIA — they are transfer payments under Secondary Income

concepts.name: Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) and Their Interaction with Current Account
key_dimensions: SDR allocations by IMF are recorded in Financial Account (increase in reserve assets), NOT Current Account
SDRs used for BoP support — countries with CAD can use SDR holdings to purchase foreign currency
2021 IMF SDR allocation of $650 billion — India received ~$17.86 billion worth
UPSC trap: SDR is not a currency and not directly usable for trade transactions — it operates between central banks/IMF, not in current transactions

concepts.name: India's Structural Current Account Deficit: Causes and Policy Responses
key_dimensions: Structural causes: high oil/gold import dependence, low export competitiveness in manufacturing, services surplus insufficient to bridge gap
Policy responses: export promotion schemes (RoDTEP, PLI), import substitution (Atmanirbhar Bharat), FTA negotiations
Cyclical vs. structural CAD distinction: cyclical CAD (due to growth/demand surge) vs. structural (supply-side deficiencies)
UPSC trap: A smaller CAD during recession is not necessarily a policy success — it may reflect demand compression rather than export improvement

concepts.name: Errors and Omissions, and Balancing Item in BoP: Relevance to Current Account Data
key_dimensions: Errors and Omissions arise due to asymmetric data collection — timing differences, under-reporting, hawala transactions
Large negative Errors and Omissions can indicate unrecorded capital flight or informal remittance channels (hawala)
RBI's BoP compilation follows IMF's Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6)
UPSC trap: BoP always balances by accounting identity — a 'BoP deficit' in common parlance refers to a fall in foreign exchange reserves, recorded under Reserve Account
